title: Le shooting de Tiffany's  (The Tiffany's Shoot)

segments.t: Before a major commercial photo shoot for Tiffany's, Sophia nurses an exhausting hangover. She confides to Camille that she drank too much after Gabriel left the agency party with his new girlfriend. Let's listen to their conversation in French first.
Tu vas bien? Tu sembles très fatiguée.
Non, je ne me sens pas bien.
Peut-on reporter ce rendez-vous photo important?
On ne reporte jamais un tel shooting!
J'ai une affreuse gueule de bois.
Ils te voient comme l'ambassadrice parfaite.
Ma féminité est plutôt à plat aujourd'hui.
Qu'est-ce qui ne va pas, Sophia?
Hier soir, Gabriel m'a plantée là.
Il est parti avec sa petite amie.
J'ai bu deux verres toute seule!
Ne sois pas jalouse, pense au travail!
D'accord, je vais assurer ce beau shooting.
Let's explore Camille and Sophia's heartfelt conversation line by line.
Tu vas bien? Tu sembles très fatiguée.
'Are you well? You seem very tired.' Camille gently observes Sophia's obvious fatigue before the shoot. Camille uses the casual singular 'you' with 'go', showing close familiarity.
Non, je ne me sens pas bien.
'No, I do not feel well.' Sophia openly acknowledges that she feels physically unwell. The two-part French negation brackets the verb for 'feel' on both sides.
Peut-on reporter ce rendez-vous photo important?
'Can we postpone this important photo shoot?' Sophia tentatively asks if the session could be delayed. Notice how 'can we' leads directly into the noun meaning 'appointment'.
On ne reporte jamais un tel shooting!
'One never postpones such a shoot!' Camille explains that prestigious fashion shoots cannot be moved. The verb meaning 'postpones' pairs naturally with the noun for 'shoot!' in everyday conversation.
J'ai une affreuse gueule de bois.
'I have an awful hangover.' Sophia admits she is suffering from a heavy morning hangover. The adjective meaning 'awful' takes its feminine form here to match the noun it describes.
Ils te voient comme l'ambassadrice parfaite.

'They see you as the perfect ambassador.' Camille reminds her that the jewelers consider her an ideal brand face. The reflexive pronoun sits right in front of the verb for 'see', turning the action back onto the subject.
Ma féminité est plutôt à plat aujourd'hui.
'My femininity is rather flat today.' Sophia laments with irony that her energy feels totally depleted. The key noun here means 'femininity', anchored by its matching French article.
Qu'est-ce qui ne va pas, Sophia?

'What is wrong, Sophia?' Camille invites her friend to share the deeper cause of her distress. Notice how the short vowel drops before a vowel sound around 'goes', making the phrase flow smoothly as one unit.
Hier soir, Gabriel m'a plantée là.

'Last night, Gabriel abandoned me there.' Sophia admits that she felt stung when Gabriel deserted her. In spoken French, the little word before 'has me' drops its final vowel and attaches with an apostrophe.
Il est parti avec sa petite amie.
'He left with his girlfriend.' Sophia explains that Gabriel walked out of the gathering with Sarah. This conversational past tense combines a helper verb with the past participle for 'left'.
J'ai bu deux verres toute seule!
'I drank two glasses all alone!' Sophia explains how she ended up finishing both ordered drinks herself. The adjective meaning 'alone!' takes its feminine form here to match the noun it describes.
Ne sois pas jalouse, pense au travail!
'Do not be jealous, think of work!' Camille urges Sophia not to let romantic jealousy derail her career. This conversational past tense combines a helper verb with the past participle for 'be'.
D'accord, je vais assurer ce beau shooting.

'All right, I will deliver on this fine shoot.' Sophia resolves to put personal feelings aside and do her best. Notice how 'am going' leads directly into the noun meaning 'shoot.'. Now let's listen to Camille and Sophia's exchange once more from start to finish.
